title: French Foreign Legion
description: French Army corps of foreign nationals
wiki_lead:
The French Foreign Legion (French: Légion étrangère, also known simply as la Légion, 'the Legion') is a corps of the French Army created to allow foreign nationals into French service. The Legion was founded in 1831 and today consists of several specialities, namely infantry, cavalry, engineers, and airborne troops. It formed part of the Armée d'Afrique, French Army units associated with France's colonial project in North Africa, until the end of the Algerian War in 1962.
Legionnaires are today renowned as highly trained soldiers whose training focuses on traditional military skills and on the Legion's strong esprit de corps, as its men come from different countries with different cultures. Consequently, training is often described as not only physically challenging, but also very stressful psychologically. Legionnaires may apply for French citizenship after three years' service, or immediately after being wounded in the line of duty; this latter provision is known as "Français par le sang versé" ("French by spilled blood").

History

The Foreign Legion was created by Louis Philippe, the King of the French, on 10 March 1831 to allow the incorporation of foreign nationals into the French Army from the foreign regiments of the Kingdom of France. Recruits included soldiers from the recently disbanded Swiss and German foreign regiments of the Bourbon monarchy and also people from shady backgrounds. The Royal Ordinance for the establishment of the new regiment specified that the foreigners recruited could only serve outside France. The French expeditionary force that had occupied Algiers in 1830 was in need of reinforcements, and the Legion was accordingly transferred by sea in detachments from Toulon to Algeria.
Since its establishment in 1831, the Legion has consisted of hundreds of thousands in active service at its peak, and suffered the aggregated loss of nearly 40,000 men in France, Morocco, Tunisia, Madagascar, West Africa, Mexico, Italy, Crimea, Spain, Indo-China, Norway, Syria, Chad, Zaïre, Lebanon, Central Africa, Gabon, Kuwait, Rwanda, Djibouti, former Yugoslavia, Somalia, the Republic of Congo, Ivory Coast, Afghanistan, Mali, as well as others. The Legion was primarily used to help protect and expand the French colonial empire during the 19th century. The Foreign Legion was initially stationed only in Algeria, where it took part in the Pacification of Algeria. Subsequently, the Foreign Legion was deployed in a number of conflicts, including the First Carlist War in 1835, the Crimean War in 1854, the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859, the French intervention in Mexico in 1863, the Franco-Prussian War in 1870, the Tonkin Campaign and Sino-French War in 1883, supporting growth of the French colonial empire in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Second Franco-Dahomean War in 1892, the Second Madagascar expedition in 1895 and the Mandingo Wars in 1894. grok_lead: The French Foreign Legion is an elite, self-contained military corps within the French Army, comprising primarily foreign volunteers who enlist under five-year contracts and serve in specialized infantry, engineering, and airborne roles, distinguished by its policy of allowing recruits to adopt a declared identity for anonymity and its ethos encapsulated in the motto Legio Patria Nostra ("The Legion is our Fatherland"). Established on 10 March 1831 by King Louis-Philippe amid post-revolutionary needs to absorb foreign elements into the military while providing manpower for the conquest of Algeria, the Legion was designed as a disposable yet reliable force for overseas expeditions, drawing from volunteers worldwide without regard to prior background provided they meet physical and age criteria (17.5 to 39.5 years). The Legion's defining characteristics include an intensely demanding four-month basic training regimen at its farm in Castelnaudary, emphasizing physical endurance, discipline, and unit cohesion, which weeds out most candidates and forges a brotherhood transcending national origins, with legionnaires swearing allegiance to the Legion itself rather than France directly. After honorable service, legionnaires become eligible for French citizenship, typically after five years or immediately if wounded in combat under the provision FranÃ§ais par le sang versÃ© ("French by spilled blood"), though applications require revelation of true identity and demonstration of integration. The force, numbering around 9,000 personnel across regiments in metropolitan France, Corsica, French Guiana, and Djibouti, maintains operational independence and has evolved from colonial shock troops to modern counterinsurgency specialists. Notable for its combat record, the Legion has engaged in over 100 campaigns, including the Crimean War, Mexican Interventionâhighlighted by the 1863 Battle of Camerone, where 65 legionnaires under Captain Danjou resisted thousands of Mexican troops for ten hours, exemplifying the creed "The Legion dies; it does not surrender "âboth World Wars, Indochina, Algeria, the Gulf War, and recent African operations against jihadists. While controversies arise from its origins in penal-like recruitment and instances of internal dissent, such as the 1961 mutiny by paratroopers opposing Algerian withdrawal, empirical outcomes affirm its causal role in French military successes through superior morale and tactical adaptability, unmarred by the narrative dilutions common in biased institutional histories.
